newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - New money brings drug problems for Indians.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New money brings drug problems for Indians.

text.p: Ved Prakash became too rich too soon, when his father sold a part of his ancestral land for the unusually large sum of 5.4 million rupees ($150,000).
That was three years ago. Today, in a drug rehabilitation centre, Prakash, writhes on an iron bed, clutching his stomach as tears stream down his face. He pleads with the doctors to help him.

"I thought God had sent the money to enjoy life, so I could enjoy things I could not when I did not have the money," he said during a brief moment of relief. "I had friends who promised to take me to heaven and I just got carried away."

Prakash, 27, whose desperate wife brought him to an addict treatment clinic, is one of many Indian addicts who made fortunes overnight from a sudden economic boom, but did not know how to cope with the unexpected windfall.
He fell victim to "brown sugar", a crude form of heroin, the preferred drug of Indian addicts.
Prakash's withdrawal symptoms are excruciating.

Gazing at the clouds far beyond the confines of his cell, he mumbles, "I thought with money and smoke I could take a walk in the sky -- but now walking on land is difficult and the sky seems to be even farther away".
The authorities say about 300,000 drug addicts annually report to the treatment centres, which usually look after urban middle class youths, and only about one-third of them manage to kick the habit.
No exact figures are available on the number of drug addicts in India, but non-governmental groups put the figure at seven to nine million in a nation of 930 million.
India has 233 counselling and awareness centres where the addicts are treated. Some 130 of these work as rehabilitation centres, a welfare ministry official said.

"These youths do not know what to do with the excess money and squander it on drinks and drugs, which has become a very serious problem for society," said Shanta Krishnan, head of the sociology department at New Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University.
The authorities are scrambling to combat the menace.
"There has been a 50 percent increase in drug seizures for the first half of 1996 as against the same period last year," Devendra Dutta, a narcotics control official, told Ruters.
Yet despite the official crackdown, drugs are not difficult to find in the right quarters because India lies on the "Golden Crescent" route of drug smugglers -- straddling Afghanistan and Pakistan.

Dutta said India is an important transit point for narcotics smuggled from the Golden Crescent to the rest of the world. Most Indian seizures were from drug-runners intercepted along the border with Pakistan, he said.
Almost all of India's drug addicts are aged between 15 and 35, the country's human resources ministry estimates.

But fewer than 10 percent make it to the rehabilitation centres, senior police officer Kiran Bedi said. She helps run Navjyoti (New Light), a non-governmental organisation that tries to cure drug addiction.
And the drop-out rate is quite high, said Bedi, who won Asia's prestigious Magsaysay award in 1994 for reform work when she ran Tihar Jail, Asia's largest, in the Indian capital.
"It all depends on the care that the programme is able to provide -- if the family of the addict is also involved then the chances of success are much higher," Bedi said.
While the drug menace has found its new clients among the rich, a majority of Indian addicts are cart pullers, manual rickshaw drivers or poor labourers.

"With a price tag of 100 rupees per gram ($80 dollars per ounce) it is a very costly habit and the addicts generally take to stealing and other petty crimes," said S.Y. Qureshi, an official with India's Human Resources ministry.

"There is a need for the banks to step in to guide the youths who have landed with a fortune due to the economic boom, on how to invest the money rather than throw it down the drain on vices like drugs," Krishnan said.
The drug menace has far-reaching effects. Studies show that 30 percent of drug addicts lose their jobs in the first year and 90 percent of them are out of work by the seventh year.
"Once you manage to kick the habit, it's like finding your way out of a living hell," said Ramesh Kumar, a former addict.
